newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian yield curve shows recession far away - study.
newsitem.headline: Belgian yield curve shows recession far away - study.

text.p: The steep Belgian yield curve shows that there is relatively little chance of a recession starting in the coming months, a university study showed.

"The current differential between long- and short-term interest rates shows that the ecomomy should be doing well in the near future. The likelihood of a recession is less than 20 percent," said Wim Fonteyne, a Ghent State University (RUG) student who won the BBL prize for best thesis in 1996.
For his thesis on "The yield curve as a business climate indicator", Fonteyne received a 150,000 franc prize from Banque Bruxelles Lambert.
Fonteyne said that the economic forecasting power of the shape of the yield curve was second only to that of the Belgian central bank's leading indicator.

A steep yield curve (where long term yields are well above short-term yields) is seen as a harbinger of strong economic growth, while a flat (short and long yields at same level) or inverted (long yields below short yields) curve is seen as a warning that a recession is nearing.

Academics have singled out several reasons for this correlation. One is hedging behavior by companies and consumers: when they expect the economy will slow down, they start saving more, thus pushing long-term yields lower. When they become optimistic again, they tend to lend money for investment, pushing long-term rates higher.
Other theories focus on the relative movement of short-term rates, notably on central bank monetary policy, which tends to hike rates in high-growth periods and vice versa.

Fonteyne said international studies show the yield curve's use as a forecasting tool is relatively limited in the short term -- one to three quarters -- but that it has a considerable forecasting power for periods of three to six quarters.

Fonteyne's dissertation analyses the forecasting value of the Belgian yield curve in the 1957-94 period. For the yield curve, he used the spread between interbank rates and bonds with maturities longer than five years. For growth, he used industrial production data, as Belgium does not have quarterly GDP growth data over such a long period.

Regression analysis shows that in the 1970-1993 period the variation in the average quarterly yield spread could explain 44 percent of the variations in cumulative growth of industrial production in the four subsequent quarters.
"As economic forecasting tools go, that is quite impressive, an only bettered by the leading indicator," Fonteyne said.

Both the leading indicator and the yield spread have the best forecasting significance for periods of four quarters, but the yield curve is more significant when trying to make forecasts about periods six to eight quarters away, he said.
Fonteyne said that when it comes to forecasting recessions, however, the yield curve can give strong indications, but has not been very accurate in recent history.

A probability study showed that when short-term rates are more than three percentage points above long rates, the chance of a recession is higher than 96 percent. This drops to 89 percent when the spread is -2, and 77 percent at a spread of -1.
When the curve is completely flat, the change of recession is 58 percent.

With long-term yields one point above short term yields, the probability of a recession falls to 38 percent, falling further to 20 percent with a two point spread and less than nine percent at positive yield spreads of three or more points.
Belgian three-month yields ended at 3.38 percent, 10-year bonds yielded 5.61 percent -- a spread of 2.23 points.
